1970 Camaro RS SS Restoration Stalled 40 Years Ago, Late Owner's Wife Finally Takes It for a Spin
94 photos
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds
What’s in a moniker worn by a car that’s been built 55 years ago, entered a restoration 40 years ago, and takes its first drive since the mid-eighties in 2026? A lifetime of treasures, memories, nostalgia, and heartfelt gratitude for a man who is no longer with us. But his spirit is, etched in the car he was prone to bring back on the road. His wife now sees it running again, courtesy of Hagerty’s Driveway Finders.
Some automotive projects carry far more weight than simple sheet metal and cast iron, serving instead as rolling monuments to lifelong love and unfinished dreams. In the latest episode of Hagerty's Driveway Finds series, hosts Dustin Hallinan and John Brito took a three-hour joyride to rescue a 1970 Chevrolet Camaro RS/SS 350.
The bronze split-bumper coupe belonged to Cindy and her late husband, fondly called “Camaro” Larry. Larry purchased the second-generation pony car in the early 1980s, and the couple actually went on their very first date inside its black vinyl cabin.
Around 1985, he decided the factory 350-cubic-inch small-block V8 was getting tired and plucked it from the engine bay to build a stronger replacement. Life intervened – and kept sidelining the project for 40 years. Despite spending eight years rebuilding the motor, Larry passed away before completing his cherished project.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Arriving in dealerships on February 26, 1970, the redesigned second-generation Camaro dropped the convertible to become a sport coupe exclusively, reaching 124,901 units for the model year. Only 12,578 buyers settled for the base 155-horsepower 250-cube inline-six. The rest of buyers (112,323 of them) ordered V8s, starting with the 200-horsepower 307 V8 small-block and the 250-horsepower L65 350-incher two-barrel V8.
Meanwhile, the $572.95 Z28 package attracted 8,733 enthusiasts with its solid-lifter 360-horsepower LT1 350-cubic-inch V8. Transmission choices across the 1970 lineup spanned a standard 3-speed manual, a 2-speed Powerglide automatic, 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic 350 or 400 automatics, and three Muncie 4-speed manual gearboxes in wide-ratio M20, close-ratio M21, or heavy-duty M22 Rock Crusher specifications.
To sharpen the coupe's European-inspired styling, 27,136 buyers ticked the box for the RPO Z22 Rally Sport package, an appearance upgrade priced at $168.55 that could be combined with any trim. That Z22 Rally Sport option replaced the standard full-width front bumper with twin split bumperettes flanking a recessed black grille framed in a resilient Endura urethane nose cone, alongside round inboard parking lamps, hideaway windshield wipers, and bright window moldings.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Meanwhile, 12,476 customers ordered the RPO Z27 Super Sport package for $289.65, which added power front disc brakes, a blacked-out grille, F70-14 white-letter tires on 14-by-7-inch wheels, hood insulation, and SS badging.
Under the hood, the base Super Sport engine was the L48 350 four-barrel V8 (also found in Larry's RS/SS), which featured a 10.25:1 compression ratio and a Rochester Quadrajet carburetor to deliver 300 horsepower at 4,800 rpm and 380 lb-ft of torque at 3,200 rpm. 10,012 car nuts went with the base SS powerhouse.
Buyers craving big-block muscle could upgrade the SS with a 402-cubic-inch big-block V8 (still badged as a 396; not to be confused with the 400-CID small-block V8), choosing either the 350-horsepower L34 for $152.75 (1,864 units) or the solid-lifter 375-horsepower L78 for $385.50 (600 copies).
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Working outside their familiar garage presented an immediate challenge for Dustin Hallinan and John Brito, who walked into a packed home workshop where they did not know where any tools or hardware were stored. The 1970 Camaro rested on a four-post lift beneath a thick layer of dust and a canvas cover buried under miscellaneous parts and spare trim pieces. Nearby sat the partially assembled V8 on a stand beside a fresh automatic transmission case.
Before turning a wrench, the duo investigated whether the powerplant on the stand was the coupe's factory-born heart. The block casting numbers and foundry date codes aligned with the production date stamped on the cowl trim tag, pointing toward an original drivetrain. Machine work during the rebuild had decked the block pad and ground away the stamped VIN derivative, but Hallinan later confirmed the automatic transmission bore the matching VIN.
Every summer, Larry and Cindy attended Hot August Nights and stopped by Summit Racing, where they admired a display motor dressed in bright orange and black. Determined to honor that exact vision, Brito masked the aluminum Edelbrock Performer RPM cylinder heads and sprayed the iron block and Chevrolet-script valve covers in vibrant orange. Meanwhile, Hallinan spent two hours wire-wheeling, sanding, and degreasing the empty engine bay before applying black paint.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds The next morning, Hallinan bypassed the factory resistance wire with a dedicated power feed to support a modern High Energy Ignition distributor. Brito poured five quarts of zinc-rich oil into the pan, sealed the black Edelbrock intake manifold, and bolted on the water pump, fuel pump, flex plate, and starter. After grinding minor clearance on the starter and priming the oil system to 60 psi using a dedicated tool, they set timing at 15 degrees.
With cast-iron exhaust manifolds bolted down using anti-seize compound (that Brito jokingly called Never-Seize), the pair indexed a brand-new torque converter into the transmission. They mated the bellhousing to the block, pre-installed the tricky transmission cooler lines, and blew out the chassis fuel line. In a poetic twist, the same red cherry picker that removed the engine 40 years ago lowered it back home.
Working underneath the lift, Hallinan marveled at how clean and rust-free the floorpans remained after four decades of indoor storage. When the first driveshaft proved too short, the guys sorted through Larry's stash of seven spare shafts out back and found the original unit. A new Brawler carburetor then suffered stripped threads from a galled aluminum fuel fitting, forcing Hallinan to salvage a donor bowl from a vintage Holley carburetor.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds After Hallinan transferred the fresh float, needle, seat, and accelerator pump into the replacement bowl and Brito installed the radiator, Cindy joined them for the initial fire-up. The small-block roared to life for the first time in 40 years, but an alarming metallic racket forced an immediate shutdown. Inspecting the exhaust collector revealed a missing intermediate pipe sleeve, which one of Larry's friends conveniently produced from his own parts stash.
Even with the exhaust sleeve installed, a loud knocking sound persisted throughout the mandatory 15-minute camshaft break-in run, during which an uncapped radiator erupted and flooded the shop floor. Pulling the driver-side valve cover and spark plugs showed zero internal damage, leaving the mechanics baffled overnight. The next morning, Brito unbolted the driver-side exhaust manifold and discovered the casting was striking the aftermarket cylinder head and an oversized head bolt.
Grinding clearance into the cast-iron manifold and stacking two thick exhaust gaskets completely eliminated the terrifying clatter, allowing the V8 to purr with a choppy camshaft lope and gear-driven timing whine. With the transmission shifting into gear on the lift, the team turned their attention to the dry rear brake reservoir. They replaced the seized rear wheel cylinders and rubber hoses, bled the brakes, and installed a fresh set of blue spark plug wires.
Photo: YouTube/Hagerty | Driveway Finds Cheered on by a gathering of Larry's friends and family, Hallinan backed the Camaro off the lift and onto public pavement for its first road test in 40 years. The fresh plug wires cured a minor ignition miss, and the coupe charged up a steep 45-degree neighborhood hill with effortless power steering and crisp shifts. In fact, the refurbished brakes grabbed so hard that they foiled Brito's celebratory burnout attempt.
After two-and-a-half days of intense wrenching, the crew bolted the sculpted hood back on, washed away 40 years of grime, and handed the keys to Cindy. Sliding behind the tilt steering wheel, she cruised the exact hometown streets she and Larry had prowled four decades ago. Calling the revival her final hurrah for her late husband, a beaming Cindy said she felt like she was in heaven right alongside him.
